terms.grammar: caedō, caedere, cecīdī, caesum with ligna (or lignum)
terms.comment: What Plautus’s masters order among the chores of the house, with sweeping and laying the couches. Splitting a log with a wedge or an axe is scindere or findere: the wood that splits well is fissile.

terms.gloss: split wood (with wedges or an axe)
evidence: Verg. G. 1.144: nam prīmī cuneīs scindēbant fissile lignum

phrases.english: We need to chop wood: winter is coming.

phrases.latin: Tata ligna secūrī findit; tū procul stā.
phrases.english: Dad is splitting logs with the axe; you stand well back.

phrases.latin: Vōs lectōs sternite. … Aliī ligna caedite, aliī piscīs dēpūrgāte
phrases.english: You lay the couches. … Some of you chop wood, others clean the fish

phrases.latin: tē cum secūrī caudicālī praeficiō prōvinciae. — At haec retūnsast.
phrases.english: You, with the axe, I put in charge of the log-splitting department. — But it’s blunt.

phrases.latin: nam prīmī cuneīs scindēbant fissile lignum
phrases.english: for the first men split their wood with wedges

sources: Lewis & Short: caedo · Lewis & Short: scindo · Lewis & Short: findo · Lewis & Short: fissilis · Lewis & Short: caudicalis
